paper_title: ReConcile: Round-Table Conference Improves Reasoning via Consensus among Diverse LLMs
paper_abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) still struggle with natural language reasoning tasks.Motivated by the society of minds (Minsky, 1988), we propose RECONCILE, a multi-model multiagent framework designed as a round table conference among diverse LLM agents.RECON-CILE enhances collaborative reasoning between LLM agents via multiple rounds of discussion, learning to convince other agents to improve their answers, and employing a confidenceweighted voting mechanism that leads to a better consensus.In each round, RECONCILE initiates discussion between agents via a 'discussion prompt' that consists of (a) grouped answers and explanations generated by each agent in the previous round, (b) their confidence scores, and (c) demonstrations of answerrectifying human explanations, used for convincing other agents.Experiments on seven benchmarks demonstrate that RECONCILE significantly improves LLMs' reasoning -both individually and as a team -surpassing prior single-agent and multi-agent baselines by up to 11.4% and even outperforming GPT-4 on three datasets.RECONCILE also flexibly incorporates different combinations of agents, including API-based, open-source, and domainspecific models, leading to an 8% improvement on MATH.Finally, we analyze the individual components of RECONCILE, demonstrating that the diversity originating from different models is critical to its superior performance. 1 Self-Refine MAD+Judge Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) ReConcile (Group-Discuss-and-Convince)Yes, with 95% confidence

prior_works.title: Improving factuality and reasoning in language models through multiagent debate
prior_works.relationship_sentence: This work is the primary multi-agent competitor that ReConcile generalizes beyond by moving from multiple copies of a single model debating to a multi-model discussion with confidence-weighted consensus and persuasion via convincing examples.

prior_works.title: Encouraging divergent thinking in large language models through multi-agent debate (and Judge)
prior_works.relationship_sentence: Liang et al. both introduced the debate+judge setup and highlighted Degeneration-of-Thought and limited diversity when agents share a backbone—gaps ReConcile addresses via diverse-model agents, explicit ‘convincing’ instruction, and consensus without a separate judge.

prior_works.title: Self-Refine: Iterative refinement with self-feedback
prior_works.relationship_sentence: Self-Refine’s self-reflection loop can stall when models are overconfident, directly motivating ReConcile’s shift to cross-model discussion and external feedback that learns to convince other agents to update incorrect answers.

prior_works.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
prior_works.relationship_sentence: ReConcile extends the self-consistency idea of aggregating multiple reasoning paths by introducing multi-model, multi-round aggregation with confidence-calibrated weighted voting instead of unweighted majority votes.

prior_works.title: LLM-Blender: Ensembling large language models with pairwise ranking and generative fusion
prior_works.relationship_sentence: While LLM-Blender shows the value of combining different LLMs’ outputs, ReConcile goes beyond static fusion by enabling interactive explanation exchange and persuasion before producing a confidence-weighted consensus.

prior_works.title: Can language models teach weaker agents? Teacher explanations improve students via theory of mind
prior_works.relationship_sentence: This work’s finding that teacher explanations can correct and improve another model’s reasoning directly inspires ReConcile’s ‘convincing samples’—answer-rectifying human explanations used in-context to teach agents to persuade peers.

prior_works.title: Society of Mind
prior_works.relationship_sentence: Minsky’s society-of-minds concept motivates ReConcile’s core idea of coordinating diverse specialized agents that communicate and collaborate to reach better solutions.

synthesis_narrative: Multi-agent debate showed that having multiple agents argue can improve factuality and reasoning, but prior implementations typically used multiple instances of the same model, limiting diversity and the scope for genuine cross-model feedback. Building on this, the debate+judge paradigm introduced a separate adjudicator and also identified Degeneration-of-Thought, where iterative processes fail to create novel reasoning when models are overconfident, reflecting a core weakness of self-reflection methods like Self-Refine. Independently, self-consistency demonstrated that sampling multiple reasoning paths and aggregating them via majority vote boosts accuracy, crystallizing the value of ensembling diverse rationales. Complementing that, LLM-Blender established that ensembling different LLMs via ranking and fusion can unlock complementary strengths across model families, though without interaction or explanation exchange. Concurrently, teacher–student work showed that explanations from a teacher can correct and improve a student’s reasoning, indicating that well-crafted explanations can actively persuade a model to revise errors. The broader conceptual backdrop comes from the society-of-minds view: complex cognition emerges from interacting specialized agents. Taken together, these strands revealed a clear opportunity: leverage genuinely diverse models to exchange explanations, explicitly learn to persuade with corrective exemplars, and then aggregate with calibrated confidence rather than an unweighted vote or an external judge. ReConcile synthesizes these insights into a round-table, multi-model, multi-round dialogue that groups stances, conditions agents on ‘convincing’ examples to generate persuasive explanations, elicits per-round confidence, and produces a confidence-weighted consensus—turning static ensembling and single-model debate into collaborative consensus-building among diverse LLMs.

innovation_classification.reasoning: Implements multi-model debate, judge, and self-consistency—an inference-time control ensemble—within a modular debate pipeline to improve reasoning.
